case: A 27-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 1-week history of malodorous vaginal discharge, vulvar itching, and pain with intercourse. She has had two new sexual partners in the past 3 months and does not use condoms. Temperature is 36.9 °C (98.4 °F). Speculum examination shows a frothy, yellow-green discharge and punctate hemorrhages on the ectocervix. Vaginal pH is 5.8 (3.8 to 4.5). Adding potassium hydroxide to the discharge releases a fishy odor. Saline wet mount shows motile, pear-shaped, flagellated organisms, many neutrophils, and squamous epithelial cells whose borders are obscured by adherent coccobacilli. Gram stain shows few lactobacilli. The diagnosis is trichomoniasis with coexisting bacterial vaginosis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the life cycle and transmission of the motile organism seen on this patient's wet mount?
options: Cyst form that survives in contaminated water
Yeast form that overgrows after antibiotic use
Trophozoite form only, passed by sexual contact
Elementary body form that enters epithelial cells
approach: Motile, pear-shaped, flagellated organisms on a saline wet mount identify Trichomonas vaginalis.
Recall its life cycle: it exists only as a trophozoite and has no cyst stage.
Without a hardy cyst it cannot survive long outside the body, so it spreads by sexual contact.
questions.why: Trichomonas vaginalis is an anaerobic flagellated protozoan that exists only as a trophozoite. It has no cyst stage, so it does not survive long in the environment and spreads mainly by sexual contact. The trophozoite attaches to squamous epithelium of the vagina, ectocervix, and male urethra and causes inflammation with many neutrophils, a frothy yellow-green discharge, a pH above 4.5, and punctate cervical hemorrhages (strawberry cervix). Men often carry it without symptoms, so sexual partners are treated as well.
whyNot: A hardy cyst passed in water or food is the infectious form of Giardia lamblia and Entamoeba histolytica. T. vaginalis has no cyst stage.
Candida albicans overgrows after antibiotics or with diabetes and causes a thick white discharge with a normal pH. It is not flagellated and does not swim.
Correct.
The elementary body is the infectious form of Chlamydia trachomatis, an obligate intracellular bacterium. It is far too small to be seen moving on a wet mount.

topics: Causes of vaginitis on wet mount

questions.stem: Which of the following findings in this patient is most specifically attributable to the bacterial vaginosis rather than to the trichomonal infection?
options: Clue cells on saline wet mount
Vaginal pH greater than 4.5
Numerous neutrophils on wet mount
Punctate hemorrhages on the ectocervix
approach: List what each condition can cause.
A pH above 4.5 and an amine odor occur in both, while neutrophils and cervical hemorrhages point to trichomoniasis.
Clue cells form when Gardnerella and anaerobes coat squamous cells, so they are specific for bacterial vaginosis.
questions.why: Bacterial vaginosis is a shift in the vaginal flora. Lactobacilli are replaced by Gardnerella vaginalis and anaerobes, which stick to squamous cells so their borders look stippled and blurred. These are clue cells. Bacterial vaginosis causes little inflammation, so neutrophils are few. Trichomoniasis also raises the pH above 4.5 and can give an amine odor, but it does not produce clue cells, so clue cells are the finding that shows bacterial vaginosis is present as well.
whyNot: Correct.
Both conditions raise vaginal pH above 4.5, so pH cannot separate them. Candidiasis is the common vaginitis with a normal pH.
Many neutrophils point to trichomoniasis, which is an inflammatory infection. Bacterial vaginosis typically has few neutrophils, which is why it is called a vaginosis.
Punctate cervical hemorrhages (strawberry cervix) come from the inflammation caused by T. vaginalis. Bacterial vaginosis does not damage the cervix in this way.

questions.stem: The Gram stain in this patient shows few lactobacilli. Loss of which of the following lactobacillus functions best explains the overgrowth of Gardnerella vaginalis and anaerobes?
options: Secretion of IgA that coats bacteria in the vaginal lumen
Release of volatile amines that kill anaerobic bacteria
Storage of glycogen within superficial squamous cells
Production of lactic acid that keeps pH at 4.5 or below
approach: Few lactobacilli means the normal protective flora has been lost.
Lactobacilli ferment epithelial glycogen products to lactic acid, which keeps the pH at 4.5 or below.
Without that acid the pH rises, and Gardnerella and anaerobes overgrow.
questions.why: Estrogen makes vaginal squamous cells store glycogen. Lactobacilli ferment the breakdown products of this glycogen into lactic acid, which keeps the vaginal pH at about 3.8 to 4.5. This acid environment holds back Gardnerella and anaerobes. When lactobacilli are lost, for example with new sexual partners or douching, the pH rises and these organisms overgrow. They then make amines that cause the fishy odor and push the pH higher still.
whyNot: Secretory IgA is made by plasma cells and carried across the epithelium by the polymeric immunoglobulin receptor. It is a host defense, and lactobacilli do not make it.
Volatile amines such as trimethylamine are made by the anaerobes of bacterial vaginosis. They cause the fishy odor and raise the pH further.
Glycogen is stored by the squamous cells under the influence of estrogen. It is the substrate that lactobacilli use, and the bacteria themselves do not store it.
Correct.

questions.stem: Trichomonads attach to the epithelium that lines this patient's vagina and ectocervix, and clue cells are shed from the same lining. Which of the following describes this epithelium?
options: Simple columnar, mucus secreting
Stratified squamous, nonkeratinized
Simple columnar, ciliated with peg cells
Stratified squamous, keratinized
approach: Clue cells are shed vaginal epithelial cells, and trichomonads attach to this same lining.
The vagina and ectocervix must resist friction, so they have a stratified squamous lining.
They are moist internal surfaces, so the epithelium is nonkeratinized.
questions.why: The vagina and ectocervix are lined by nonkeratinized stratified squamous epithelium whose cells store glycogen under estrogen. This is the surface that T. vaginalis attaches to and the source of clue cells in bacterial vaginosis. The endocervical canal is lined by mucus-secreting simple columnar epithelium. The two meet at the transformation zone, where columnar cells are replaced by squamous metaplasia and where cervical dysplasia begins.
whyNot: Mucus-secreting simple columnar epithelium lines the endocervical canal. It meets the squamous epithelium of the ectocervix at the transformation zone.
Correct.
Ciliated simple columnar epithelium with secretory peg cells lines the uterine tube, where the cilia help move the oocyte toward the uterus.
Keratinized stratified squamous epithelium covers the skin, including the labia majora. The vaginal lining stays moist and does not keratinize under normal conditions.

case: A 19-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department because of a 1-day history of fever, vomiting, watery diarrhea, muscle aches, and lightheadedness on standing. She is on day 3 of her menstrual period and has used high-absorbency tampons; the most recent was placed about 20 hours ago. Temperature is 39.8 °C (103.6 °F), pulse is 128/min, respirations are 24/min, and blood pressure is 78/44 mmHg. She has a diffuse, blanching, erythematous macular rash and bilateral conjunctival hyperemia. A retained tampon is removed during pelvic examination. Laboratory studies show a platelet count of 88,000/mm3 (150,000 to 400,000), serum creatinine of 2.1 mg/dL (0.6 to 1.1), and creatine kinase of 1,850 U/L (30 to 170). Blood cultures show no growth. Vaginal culture grows Staphylococcus aureus. The diagnosis is menstrual toxic shock syndrome.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains this patient's hypotension and multiorgan injury?
options: Lipopolysaccharide binding to TLR4 on macrophages
Cytokine surge from mass T cell activation
Bloodstream spread of bacteria into many organs
Immune complex deposition in small blood vessels
approach: Note fever, shock, a diffuse rash, and injury to several organs, with negative blood cultures and a retained tampon.
This pattern fits a toxin absorbed from a local S. aureus infection.
TSST-1 is a superantigen, so it activates huge numbers of T cells and causes a cytokine storm.
questions.why: TSST-1 is a superantigen made by S. aureus growing on the retained tampon. It activates a large fraction of T cells at once, and they release large amounts of IL-2, interferon-gamma, and TNF-alpha, which push macrophages to release IL-1 and more TNF-alpha. This cytokine storm causes fever, vasodilation, capillary leak, and hypotension, with injury to the kidneys and muscle and a fall in the platelet count. Blood cultures are usually negative because the toxin is absorbed from the vagina and bacteremia is not needed. A diffuse rash appears early, and the palms and soles peel 1 to 2 weeks later.
whyNot: Lipopolysaccharide binding to TLR4 drives septic shock from gram-negative bacteria. S. aureus is gram-positive and has no lipopolysaccharide.
Correct.
Her blood cultures are negative. Menstrual toxic shock syndrome comes from toxin absorbed from a local vaginal infection, without spread of bacteria through the blood.
Immune complex deposition (type III hypersensitivity) causes vasculitis and glomerulonephritis that develop over days to weeks, as in serum sickness. It does not cause shock within a day.

questions.stem: Which of the following binding interactions of the toxin explains why it activates such a large fraction of this patient's T cells?
options: Peptide bound in the MHC class I groove presented to CD8 T cells
CD28 on T cells, in place of the B7 costimulatory molecule
Peptide bound in the MHC class II groove after endocytosis
MHC class II and TCR V-beta, outside the peptide groove
approach: Activation of a huge share of T cells at once means the toxin bypasses antigen specificity.
Specificity comes from the peptide in the MHC groove, so the toxin must bind outside it.
TSST-1 links MHC class II to the V-beta region of the T cell receptor.
questions.why: A conventional antigen is processed into peptides that sit in the MHC groove, and only the rare T cells with a matching receptor respond, far fewer than 1 in 1,000. TSST-1 acts as an intact protein and is never processed into peptides. It binds the outside of MHC class II on antigen-presenting cells and the V-beta region of the T cell receptor, away from the peptide groove. Every T cell that uses a matching V-beta family is activated, which can be up to about 20% of all T cells, so cytokine release is massive.
whyNot: MHC class I presents processed peptides from inside the cell to CD8 T cells. This is antigen specific and activates only a few clones.

CD28 binding to B7 provides the second signal for T cell activation. A costimulatory signal on its own does not activate a T cell and does not explain why so many clones respond. The huge response comes from binding the V-beta region of the T cell receptor.
This is normal presentation of an extracellular protein to CD4 T cells. Only T cells specific for that peptide respond, so the number activated is small.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following hormonal events most directly started the menstrual bleeding during which this patient used the tampons?
options: Fall in progesterone as the corpus luteum regresses
Surge in LH caused by positive feedback from estradiol
Rise in FSH that recruits the next cohort of follicles
Rise in estradiol secreted by the dominant follicle
approach: Menses is shedding of the functional layer of the endometrium.
The secretory endometrium depends on progesterone from the corpus luteum.
Without hCG the corpus luteum regresses, progesterone falls, and the lining is shed.
questions.why: After ovulation, the corpus luteum secretes progesterone and estrogen, which convert the proliferative endometrium into secretory endometrium. Without pregnancy and hCG, the corpus luteum regresses after about 14 days. The fall in progesterone causes spiral artery constriction, ischemia, and shedding of the functional layer, which is menses. The luteal phase stays near 14 days because the corpus luteum has a fixed lifespan, so differences in cycle length come from the follicular phase.
whyNot: Correct.
The LH surge occurs at mid cycle and triggers ovulation about a day later. It starts the luteal phase and does not cause menses.
FSH rises late in the luteal phase as estrogen and progesterone fall, recruiting follicles for the next cycle. It accompanies menses but does not cause the endometrium to shed.
Rising estradiol in the follicular phase builds the proliferative endometrium. It thickens the lining and does not shed it.

questions.stem: Which of the following changes in the vaginal environment during menstruation most favored growth of S. aureus and toxin production in this patient?
options: Increase in lactic acid made by lactobacilli
Rise in epithelial glycogen from high estrogen
Rise in vaginal pH from menstrual blood
Greater secretion of IgA into cervical mucus
approach: Recall the normal vaginal defense: lactobacilli make lactic acid that keeps the pH at 4.5 or below.
Menstrual blood has a pH near 7.4 and buffers this acid.
A near-neutral pH, with oxygen brought in by the tampon, lets S. aureus grow and make TSST-1.
questions.why: Lactobacilli keep vaginal pH at about 3.8 to 4.5 with lactic acid, and this acid limits growth of S. aureus and many other organisms. Menstrual blood has a pH near 7.4 and buffers that acid, so the vaginal pH rises toward neutral during menses. A high-absorbency tampon left in place also brings in oxygen and holds blood as a growth medium. A near-neutral pH and oxygen favor S. aureus growth and TSST-1 production.
whyNot: More lactic acid would lower the pH and protect against S. aureus. Menstrual blood has the opposite effect.
Epithelial glycogen rises with estrogen in the follicular and ovulatory phases. Estrogen is low during menses, and more glycogen would feed lactobacilli and keep the pH low.
Correct.
Secretory IgA is a mucosal defense that blocks microbial attachment. An increase would help protect her from infection.

topics: Risk factors for menstrual toxic shock

case: A 31-year-old woman comes to the physician 3 weeks after delivering her first child because of a 2-day history of pain and redness in the right breast, fever, and chills. She is breastfeeding and has had a painful crack in the right nipple for 1 week. Temperature is 38.9 °C (102.0 °F), pulse is 104/min, respirations are 16/min, and blood pressure is 118/72 mmHg. The upper outer quadrant of the right breast has a warm, tender, wedge-shaped area of erythema without fluctuance. A smooth, mobile, nontender, 2-cm cystic mass is present beneath the left areola, and aspiration yields thick, milky fluid. Leukocyte count is 14,200/mm3 (4,500 to 11,000). Culture of milk from the right breast is pending. The diagnosis is acute lactational mastitis of the right breast with a galactocele of the left breast.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the organism most likely to grow from the milk culture and its route into the breast?
options: Catalase-negative cocci in chains carried in blood from the uterus
Lactose-fermenting gram-negative rods spread from the infant's gut
Anaerobic organisms growing behind keratin-plugged lactiferous ducts
Coagulase-positive cocci in clusters entering a nipple fissure
approach: A breastfeeding woman with a cracked nipple, fever, and a red, warm, wedge-shaped area has acute mastitis.
Organisms from the skin and the infant's mouth enter through the fissure.
The usual cause is S. aureus: gram-positive cocci in clusters that are catalase and coagulase positive.
questions.why: Acute mastitis in the first weeks of breastfeeding is usually caused by Staphylococcus aureus, a gram-positive coccus that grows in clusters and is catalase and coagulase positive. Organisms from the skin or the infant's mouth enter through cracks and fissures in the nipple. Milk stasis in the affected lobes helps them grow. The breast becomes red, warm, and painful with fever, and untreated infection can form an abscess that feels fluctuant.
whyNot: Streptococci can cause postpartum uterine infection, but lactational mastitis comes from skin and mouth organisms entering through the nipple. Spread through the blood from the uterus is not the usual route.
Gram-negative rods such as E. coli are uncommon causes of lactational mastitis. They are the usual cause of urinary tract infections.
Keratin-plugged ducts with squamous metaplasia describe periductal mastitis in smokers, which often involves mixed flora. It is a subareolar process unrelated to breastfeeding.
Correct.

questions.stem: If the cystic mass beneath this patient's left areola ruptured, which of the following would most likely result?
options: Malignant change in the epithelium lining the cyst
Local inflammation from milk leaking into the stroma
Squamous metaplasia with keratin plugging of the duct
Hemorrhagic infarction of the surrounding lobules
approach: A milky aspirate from a smooth subareolar cyst in a lactating woman identifies a galactocele.
Its contents are milk, which irritates tissue once it leaves the duct.
Rupture therefore causes a local inflammatory reaction.
questions.why: A galactocele is a cystic dilation of a duct filled with milk. It forms when a duct is blocked during lactation or weaning. Milk is irritating once it leaves the duct. If the cyst ruptures, milk lipids and proteins enter the stroma and set off a local inflammatory reaction, which can leave a firm area or scar. A galactocele is benign and does not become malignant.
whyNot: A galactocele is a benign retention cyst with no precancerous potential.
Correct.
Squamous metaplasia with keratin plugs is the cause of periductal mastitis, which is linked to smoking.
Rupture of a milk cyst does not block the blood supply of the lobules. Infarction of breast tissue is rare and is not a result of a galactocele.

questions.stem: Which of the following is required for the alveolar cells of this patient's breasts to synthesize the main carbohydrate in her milk?
options: Lactase on the apical membrane acting in reverse
Aldose reductase converting glucose into galactose
Alpha-lactalbumin bound to galactosyltransferase
Sucrase-isomaltase linking glucose to galactose
approach: The main carbohydrate in milk is lactose, made from UDP-galactose and glucose.
Galactosyltransferase on its own prefers proteins as acceptors.
Alpha-lactalbumin binds it to form lactose synthase, which uses glucose.
questions.why: Lactose is made in the Golgi of mammary alveolar cells from UDP-galactose and glucose. The enzyme galactosyltransferase normally adds galactose to glycoproteins. Alpha-lactalbumin, a whey protein whose synthesis rises under prolactin, binds the enzyme and greatly lowers its Km for glucose, so the pair makes lactose. Together they are called lactose synthase. Human milk is high in lactose, whey proteins, and secretory IgA but low in vitamin D and vitamin K, which is why newborns receive vitamin K at birth and breastfed infants receive vitamin D.
whyNot: Lactase on the small intestinal brush border splits lactose into glucose and galactose. It does not make lactose in the breast.
Aldose reductase reduces glucose to sorbitol and galactose to galactitol. The conversion between glucose and galactose uses UDP-glucose 4-epimerase.
Correct.
Sucrase-isomaltase is an intestinal brush border enzyme that digests sucrose and alpha-limit dextrins. It has no role in milk synthesis.

questions.stem: This patient notices milk dripping from her left breast when she hears her infant cry, before the infant begins to nurse. Which of the following best explains this response?
options: Oxytocin release causing myoepithelial cell contraction
Prolactin release causing myoepithelial cell contraction
Prolactin release increasing alveolar milk synthesis
Dopamine release relaxing smooth muscle of the sinuses
approach: Milk leaving the breast within seconds is ejection of milk that is already stored.
Ejection needs contraction of the myoepithelial cells around the alveoli.
Oxytocin from the posterior pituitary does this, and the reflex can become conditioned to the infant's cry.
questions.why: Milk ejection (let-down) is a neuroendocrine reflex. Suckling, and after conditioning the sight or sound of the infant, activates hypothalamic neurons in the paraventricular and supraoptic nuclei, which release oxytocin from the posterior pituitary. Oxytocin contracts the myoepithelial cells around the alveoli and pushes stored milk into the ducts within about a minute. Prolactin from the anterior pituitary rises with suckling and drives milk synthesis for later feedings. High prolactin during regular suckling also suppresses GnRH, which delays the return of ovulation.
whyNot: Correct.
Prolactin acts on alveolar epithelial cells to make milk. It has no contractile effect on myoepithelial cells.
Prolactin-driven synthesis refills the alveoli over hours. It does not explain milk dripping within seconds of a cry, before any suckling.
Hypothalamic dopamine tonically inhibits prolactin release from the anterior pituitary. It does not act on the breast to release milk.

dx: Traumatic fat necrosis of the breast
case: A 52-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a firm lump in her left breast that she noticed 2 weeks ago. Eight weeks ago she was the restrained driver in a motor vehicle collision, and the seat belt left a large bruise across the left breast. She has no nipple discharge. Examination shows a 2-cm firm, irregular, nontender mass in the upper inner quadrant of the left breast with dimpling of the overlying skin. There is no axillary lymphadenopathy. Mammography shows an irregular density with calcifications. Core needle biopsy shows necrotic adipocytes surrounded by lipid-laden foamy macrophages, multinucleated giant cells, and calcium deposits, with early fibrosis and no atypical epithelial cells. The diagnosis is traumatic fat necrosis of the breast.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the calcifications seen on this patient's mammogram?
options: Dystrophic calcification of necrotic fat cells
Metastatic calcification from high serum calcium
Calcification of necrotic tumor debris in ducts
Calcium oxalate crystals in apocrine cyst fluid
approach: The biopsy shows dead fat cells with calcium deposits in a woman with a recent breast injury.
Calcium that settles in dead tissue while serum calcium is normal is dystrophic calcification.
In fat necrosis, fatty acids from the dead fat cells bind calcium.
questions.why: Trauma ruptures fat cells, and the released lipid and dead cells draw in foamy macrophages and multinucleated giant cells. Fatty acids from the dead fat cells combine with calcium, which is dystrophic calcification: calcium deposits in dead tissue while the serum calcium is normal. Fibrosis follows. In the breast this is called nonenzymatic fat necrosis because it is started by trauma, unlike the enzymatic fat necrosis of acute pancreatitis. The firm mass, skin dimpling, and calcifications can look like carcinoma on exam and mammography, so a biopsy is needed.
whyNot: Correct.

Metastatic calcification occurs in normal tissues such as the kidney, lung, and gastric mucosa when serum calcium or phosphate is high. Nothing here suggests hypercalcemia, and the calcium sits in dead fat.
Calcified necrotic debris inside ducts is typical of comedo-type ductal carcinoma in situ. The biopsy shows no atypical epithelial cells.
Calcium oxalate crystals can form in benign apocrine cysts. The biopsy here shows necrotic fat and no cysts.

topics: Traumatic fat necrosis of the breast

questions.stem: Mammary duct ectasia was in the differential diagnosis. In a 67-year-old multiparous woman with that condition, biopsy shows dilated subareolar ducts filled with thick secretions and a periductal infiltrate rich in plasma cells. Which of the following best explains the nipple retraction that often develops in that condition?
options: Carcinoma cells infiltrating the suspensory ligaments
Dermal edema from blocked lymphatic vessels
Fibrosis that follows chronic periductal inflammation
Contraction of hypertrophied areolar smooth muscle
approach: Dilated ducts with thick secretions and plasma cell-rich inflammation describe mammary duct ectasia.
Chronic inflammation heals by fibrosis.
Contracting periductal scar tissue pulls the nipple inward and can mimic carcinoma.
questions.why: In duct ectasia, thick, lipid-rich secretions collect in dilated subareolar ducts and leak into the surrounding tissue. This causes chronic inflammation with many plasma cells, lymphocytes, and macrophages. The inflammation heals by fibrosis, which shortens the tissue around the ducts and pulls the nipple inward. Nipple retraction, a subareolar mass, and thick discharge can mimic carcinoma, so tissue diagnosis is needed. The condition is most often seen in older multiparous women.
whyNot: Carcinoma involving the suspensory ligaments causes skin dimpling and can retract the nipple, but this biopsy shows inflammation and no tumor.
Blocked dermal lymphatics cause skin edema with peau d'orange, as in inflammatory carcinoma. Edema swells the skin and does not pull the nipple inward.
Correct.
Areolar smooth muscle contracts to make the nipple erect. It does not hypertrophy in duct ectasia, and its contraction does not invert the nipple.

questions.stem: Periductal mastitis was also considered. A 36-year-old woman who smokes one pack of cigarettes daily and is not pregnant or breastfeeding has a painful, red subareolar mass that drains pus at the edge of the areola. Which of the following changes in her lactiferous ducts most likely began this process?
options: Dilation with thick lipid-rich secretions
Squamous metaplasia with keratin plugging
Papillary growth on fibrovascular cores
Infection entering through nipple fissures
approach: A smoker with a painful subareolar mass and a draining tract at the areolar edge has periductal mastitis.
Smoking is linked to squamous metaplasia of the lactiferous duct lining.
Keratin plugs the duct, and rupture releases keratin that provokes inflammation and abscess.
questions.why: Periductal mastitis is strongly linked to smoking. The lining of the lactiferous ducts undergoes squamous metaplasia, and the squamous cells shed keratin that plugs and dilates the duct. When the duct ruptures, keratin leaks into the stroma and causes intense inflammation, which forms a painful subareolar mass or abscess. The abscess can drain through a fistula that opens at the edge of the areola.
whyNot: Dilated ducts with thick secretions and plasma cell-rich inflammation describe mammary duct ectasia, which is seen mainly in older multiparous women.
Correct.
Papillary fronds on fibrovascular cores inside a duct form an intraductal papilloma, which causes bloody nipple discharge without signs of infection.
Infection through nipple fissures causes acute lactational mastitis in breastfeeding women. This woman is not breastfeeding, and her risk factor is smoking.

questions.stem: The dimpling of the skin over this patient's mass is most likely caused by fibrous scarring that shortens which of the following structures?
options: Lactiferous ducts converging on the nipple
Pectoral fascia under the retromammary space
Subdermal lymphatic plexus of the breast
Suspensory ligaments of the breast
approach: Skin dimpling means something is pulling the dermis toward the mass.
The suspensory ligaments connect the deep fascia to the dermis.
Fibrosis from fat necrosis or carcinoma shortens these ligaments and tethers the skin.
questions.why: The suspensory (Cooper) ligaments are bands of connective tissue that run from the deep fascia through the breast to the dermis. When scar tissue or tumor involves them, they shorten and pull the skin inward, which produces dimpling. Both carcinoma and benign scarring such as fat necrosis can do this, so dimpling alone cannot separate them. The breast lies on the pectoralis major from about rib 2 to rib 6, separated from the pectoral fascia by the retromammary space, and has an axillary tail that extends toward the axilla.
whyNot: Shortening of the lactiferous ducts near the nipple causes nipple retraction. It does not dimple skin away from the nipple.
Involvement of the pectoral fascia fixes a mass to the chest wall so it does not move when the pectoralis major contracts. It does not pull on the skin.
Blocked subdermal lymphatics cause edema with peau d'orange, a pitted, thickened skin. They do not produce focal dimpling.
Correct.

dx: Fibroadenoma in a young woman, with phyllodes tumor as the differential
case: A 23-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a painless lump in her left breast that she noticed 2 months ago while showering. It has not changed in size. She has no nipple discharge and no family history of breast cancer. Examination shows a 2.5-cm firm, rubbery, smooth, nontender mass in the upper outer quadrant of the left breast that moves freely under the examining fingers. There is no skin change or axillary lymphadenopathy. Ultrasonography shows an oval, well-circumscribed, solid mass. Core needle biopsy shows proliferating stroma of low cellularity compressing ducts into slit-like spaces, with no stromal mitoses. The ducts are lined by an inner luminal cell layer and an outer cell layer. The diagnosis is fibroadenoma.

questions.stem: This patient becomes pregnant 1 year later. Which of the following changes in the mass is most likely during the pregnancy?
options: Regression as prolactin suppresses estrogen
Involution with stromal calcification
Enlargement driven by rising estrogen
Transformation into invasive carcinoma
approach: Fibroadenoma contains hormone-responsive stroma and ducts.
Pregnancy brings very high estrogen from the placenta.
The tumor therefore tends to enlarge, while it shrinks and calcifies after menopause.
questions.why: A fibroadenoma is a benign proliferation of the specialized intralobular stroma together with ducts. Both parts respond to ovarian hormones, so fibroadenomas can grow during pregnancy and lactation, when estrogen levels are very high. After menopause, as estrogen falls, they tend to shrink and often calcify. Fibroadenoma is the most common benign breast tumor in young women and almost never becomes malignant.
whyNot: Prolactin rises in pregnancy, but the placenta makes very large amounts of estrogen. Suppression of the ovarian axis does not lower estrogen while the placenta is producing it.
Involution with coarse calcification happens after menopause, when estrogen is low.
Correct.
Fibroadenoma has little or no malignant potential, and pregnancy does not convert it into carcinoma.

topics: Hormone effects on benign breast tumors

questions.stem: Which of the following biopsy findings, had it been present, would have favored a phyllodes tumor over fibroadenoma?
options: Single-file strands of discohesive cells
Ducts compressed into slits by bland stroma
Papillae with fibrovascular cores in a duct
Leaflike fronds of hypercellular stroma
approach: Phyllodes tumor and fibroadenoma both mix stroma and ducts, so look at the stroma.
Phyllodes stroma is hypercellular and outgrows the epithelium.
The overgrown stroma bulges into clefts as leaf-like fronds, which is the key feature.
questions.why: Fibroadenoma and phyllodes tumor are both fibroepithelial tumors, and in both the stroma is the neoplastic part. In phyllodes tumor, the stroma is more cellular, may show mitoses and atypia, and grows faster than the epithelium, so it bulges into epithelium-lined clefts as leaf-like projections. Phyllodes tumors usually occur in older women, most often in the sixth decade, and they can grow large, recur after excision, and in high-grade cases spread through the blood. Fibroadenoma has bland stroma of low cellularity, as in this patient.
whyNot: Single-file strands of discohesive cells are typical of invasive lobular carcinoma, an epithelial cancer.
Ducts compressed into slits by bland, low-cellularity stroma are the pattern of fibroadenoma, which this patient already has.
Papillary fronds with fibrovascular cores inside a large duct describe an intraductal papilloma.
Correct.

questions.stem: The epithelial part of this patient's tumor arises from the same structure in which most breast carcinomas begin. Which of the following describes that structure?
options: Terminal duct joined to a cluster of acini
Lactiferous duct opening at the nipple surface
Lactiferous sinus just beneath the areola
Areolar gland that secretes oily sebum
approach: Fibroadenomas contain both specialized stroma and epithelium of the lobule.
The unit where most breast cancers start is the terminal duct lobular unit.
It consists of a terminal duct and the cluster of small acini it drains.
questions.why: The terminal duct lobular unit is a terminal duct with its cluster of small ductules (acini) and the loose specialized stroma around them. Its epithelium has two layers: inner luminal cells and outer myoepithelial cells on the basement membrane. Most breast carcinomas, both ductal and lobular, begin in this unit, and fibroadenomas arise from its stroma and epithelium. The large ducts and lactiferous sinuses near the nipple are the usual site of intraductal papillomas.
whyNot: Correct.
Large lactiferous ducts carry milk to the nipple. They are the usual site of intraductal papilloma and periductal mastitis, and few carcinomas or fibroadenomas begin there.
The lactiferous sinus is the widened part of a large duct under the areola, where milk collects. Fibroadenomas do not arise here.
Areolar (Montgomery) glands are modified sebaceous glands that lubricate the nipple. They are not the source of these tumors.

questions.stem: Fibroadenoma contains ducts and stroma that respond to ovarian steroids in the same way as normal breast tissue. Which of the following correctly pairs each hormone with its main effect on normal breast development?
options: Progesterone drives duct growth, estrogen drives lobular growth
Estrogen drives duct growth, progesterone drives lobular growth
Estrogen drives duct growth, testosterone drives lobular growth
Testosterone drives duct growth, progesterone drives lobular growth
approach: At puberty the breast first grows ducts under rising estrogen.
Lobules and alveoli expand with progesterone in luteal phases and in pregnancy.
Androgens oppose breast growth, so they fit neither role.
questions.why: At puberty, estrogen stimulates growth and branching of the ducts and deposition of fat and stroma. Progesterone, made by the corpus luteum each cycle and in large amounts in pregnancy, adds growth of the lobules and alveoli. Full development of milk-making alveoli also needs prolactin. Androgens oppose breast growth, which is why breast enlargement in men follows a rise in the estrogen to androgen ratio.
whyNot: This reverses the two roles. Estrogen is the main driver of duct growth, and progesterone is needed for development of lobules and alveoli.
Correct.
Testosterone does not promote lobular growth. Androgens oppose breast growth.
Duct growth is driven by estrogen. Androgens oppose breast growth and do not drive duct development.

topics: Estrogen and progesterone effects on the breast

dx: Intraductal papilloma with bloody nipple discharge in a woman with fibrocystic breast change
case: A 44-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 3-week history of spontaneous bloody discharge from the right nipple. For several years both breasts have felt lumpy and tender in the week before menses. Her menses are regular. Pressure at the edge of the right areola at the 9 o'clock position produces bloody discharge from a single duct orifice. No discrete mass is palpable. Serum prolactin is 12 ng/mL (less than 25). Ultrasonography shows a 6-mm solid mass inside a dilated subareolar duct and several simple cysts in both breasts. Excision of the duct shows papillary fronds with fibrovascular cores. Biopsy of one cyst shows apocrine metaplasia of its lining and surrounding stromal fibrosis without epithelial hyperplasia. The diagnosis is intraductal papilloma with nonproliferative fibrocystic change.

questions.stem: Which of the following histologic features of this patient's duct lesion best distinguishes it from papillary carcinoma?
options: Fibrovascular cores within the papillae
Myoepithelial cells along the papillae
Location within a large subareolar duct
Red blood cells within the duct lumen
approach: Both papilloma and papillary carcinoma form fronds with fibrovascular cores inside a duct.
Benign duct lesions keep the normal two-layer lining of luminal and myoepithelial cells.
A myoepithelial layer along the papillae therefore points to papilloma.
questions.why: An intraductal papilloma is a benign papillary growth inside a large subareolar duct. It is a common cause of spontaneous bloody discharge from a single duct, often with no palpable mass. Each papilla has a fibrovascular core covered by the same two cell layers as a normal duct, luminal cells and myoepithelial cells. Papillary carcinoma also has fibrovascular cores but has lost the myoepithelial layer along its papillae, so finding that layer supports a benign lesion.
whyNot: Fibrovascular cores are present in both papilloma and papillary carcinoma. They show that the lesion is papillary without showing whether it is benign.
Correct.
Both benign and malignant papillary lesions can occur in large ducts, so location does not separate them.
Bleeding into the duct occurs with both papilloma and papillary carcinoma, so it cannot tell them apart.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the breast cancer risk associated with the type of fibrocystic change found in this patient's cyst biopsy, compared with the general population?
options: No increase in risk
About 1.5 to 2 times higher
About 4 to 5 times higher
About 8 to 10 times higher
approach: Classify the change by what the epithelium is doing: cysts, apocrine metaplasia, and fibrosis are nonproliferative.
Nonproliferative change carries no added cancer risk.
Risk rises only with epithelial proliferation, and more with atypia.
questions.why: Fibrocystic change is graded by how much the epithelium proliferates. Nonproliferative change, which includes cysts, apocrine metaplasia, and stromal fibrosis as in this patient, does not raise cancer risk. Proliferative change without atypia, such as epithelial hyperplasia, sclerosing adenosis, and intraductal papilloma, raises risk slightly, about 1.5 to 2 times. Atypical ductal or lobular hyperplasia raises risk about 4 to 5 times.
whyNot: Correct.
A slight increase of about 1.5 to 2 times goes with proliferative change without atypia, such as epithelial hyperplasia, sclerosing adenosis, or an intraductal papilloma.
A moderate increase of about 4 to 5 times goes with atypical ductal or atypical lobular hyperplasia.
A risk of about 8 to 10 times goes with carcinoma in situ, such as lobular or ductal carcinoma in situ.

questions.stem: Hyperprolactinemia was considered before her prolactin level was measured. If a prolactin-secreting pituitary adenoma were present, which of the following would most likely disrupt her menstrual cycles?
options: Prolactin blockade of endometrial estrogen receptors
Stalk compression raising gonadotropin release
Prolactin-induced destruction of ovarian follicles
Suppression of pulsatile GnRH secretion
approach: Prolactin is under tonic dopamine inhibition, and a prolactinoma secretes it without that control.
High prolactin suppresses pulsatile GnRH release from the hypothalamus.
Low LH and FSH stop ovulation and disrupt menses.
questions.why: Prolactin is the anterior pituitary hormone held mainly under inhibition, by hypothalamic dopamine acting on lactotrophs. High prolactin suppresses pulsatile GnRH release from the hypothalamus. LH and FSH fall, follicles do not mature, ovulation stops, and estrogen is low, which causes oligomenorrhea or amenorrhea, often with galactorrhea. Galactorrhea from hyperprolactinemia is usually milky and from both breasts, while this patient's bloody discharge from a single duct points to a duct lesion.
whyNot: Prolactin does not block estrogen receptors in the endometrium. Menses become irregular because ovulation stops.
Stalk compression interrupts dopamine delivery and raises prolactin. Gonadotropin release falls, because it depends on GnRH reaching the pituitary through the same portal vessels.
Follicles are preserved in hyperprolactinemia. They fail to mature because gonadotropins are low, and cycles return once prolactin falls.
Correct.

questions.stem: Examination also shows a 4-mm pigmented papule with a small central nipple-like projection on the left upper abdomen, directly below the left nipple. Which of the following best explains this finding?
options: Failed fusion of paired mesodermal breast primordia
Migration of neural crest melanocytes into dermis
Partial persistence of the ectodermal mammary ridge
Persistence of a remnant of the vitelline duct
approach: A small nipple-like papule in line with the nipple suggests a supernumerary nipple.
The breast forms from the ectodermal mammary ridge that runs from the axilla to the groin.
Parts of the ridge that fail to regress can form extra nipples or breast tissue along this line.
questions.why: During the embryonic period, a band of thickened ectoderm called the mammary ridge (milk line) runs on each side from the axilla to the inguinal region. Normally it disappears except in the pectoral region, where the breast develops. If other parts persist, a supernumerary nipple (polythelia) or extra breast tissue can form anywhere along this line, most often just below the normal breast.
whyNot: Each breast forms from a single ectodermal bud on the mammary ridge. Breasts do not form by fusion of paired primordia.
Neural crest melanocytes in the dermis form pigmented lesions such as a blue nevus or a congenital dermal melanocytosis. They do not form a nipple-like structure along the milk line.
Correct.
A vitelline duct remnant can leave an umbilical polyp, sinus, or Meckel diverticulum. It appears at the umbilicus and not in line with the nipple.

dx: Invasive ductal carcinoma with Paget disease of the nipple
case: A 58-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a 4-month history of an itchy, red, scaly, crusted rash on the left nipple and areola that has not improved with a topical corticosteroid. Examination shows erythema, scaling, and a small erosion of the left nipple and areola. A 2.5-cm hard, irregular, fixed mass is palpated in the lower inner quadrant of the left breast, and a firm 1.5-cm left axillary lymph node is palpable. Mammography shows a spiculated mass and fine linear branching calcifications extending toward the nipple. Biopsy of the nipple shows large cells with abundant pale cytoplasm and prominent nucleoli, single and in clusters, within the epidermis. Core biopsy of the mass shows invasive ductal carcinoma with adjacent ductal carcinoma in situ. The tumor is negative for estrogen and progesterone receptors and strongly positive (3+) for HER2. The diagnosis is invasive ductal carcinoma with Paget disease of the nipple.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the origin of the large cells in this patient's nipple epidermis?
options: Epidermal keratinocytes undergoing malignant change in place
Melanocytes proliferating along the epidermal basal layer
Langerhans cells infiltrating the epidermis from dermis
Ductal carcinoma cells spreading through lactiferous ducts
approach: An eczema-like nipple rash that does not respond to steroids, with a breast mass, suggests Paget disease.
Large pale cells within the epidermis are Paget cells.
They are carcinoma cells that reached the skin by spreading through the lactiferous ducts from the underlying ductal cancer.
questions.why: In Paget disease of the nipple, cells from an underlying ductal carcinoma spread along the lactiferous ducts into the skin of the nipple without crossing the epidermal basement membrane. Paget cells are large, with abundant pale or clear cytoplasm, and lie within the epidermis. They disrupt the skin barrier and cause an eczema-like rash with scaling and crusting that does not respond to steroids. Nearly all cases have an underlying carcinoma, either ductal carcinoma in situ or invasive ductal carcinoma, and the Paget cells usually share its HER2 overexpression.
whyNot: Malignant change of keratinocytes in place is squamous cell carcinoma in situ (Bowen disease). Its atypical keratinocytes are not linked to an underlying ductal carcinoma.
Melanoma in situ spreads along the basal layer as atypical melanocytes. It does not come with an underlying ductal carcinoma.

Langerhans cells are dendritic antigen-presenting cells that normally live in the epidermis. They increase in some forms of dermatitis and in Langerhans cell histiocytosis and are not malignant breast epithelial cells.
Correct.

questions.stem: Which of the following findings would best show that this patient's breast tumor has progressed beyond carcinoma in situ?
options: Comedo necrosis in involved ducts
Fine linear branching calcifications
Tumor nests in desmoplastic stroma
High-grade nuclei with many mitoses
approach: What separates in situ from invasive carcinoma is the basement membrane.
Comedo necrosis, linear calcifications, and high grade can all occur in ductal carcinoma in situ.
Tumor cells in stroma with a desmoplastic reaction prove invasion.
questions.why: Ductal carcinoma in situ stays within ducts, bounded by the myoepithelial cells and basement membrane. It often shows comedo necrosis and fine linear or branching calcifications on mammography, and it may be high grade, but it cannot spread through lymphatics or blood. Invasive ductal carcinoma has broken through the basement membrane into the stroma, where tumor cells provoke a dense fibrous (desmoplastic) reaction. This reaction is why the mass is hard, irregular, and spiculated. Invasive ductal carcinoma is the most common type of invasive breast cancer.
whyNot: Comedo necrosis is central necrosis in ducts filled with high-grade ductal carcinoma in situ. It is a feature of in situ disease.
Fine linear branching calcifications form in necrotic debris inside ducts and are the classic mammographic sign of ductal carcinoma in situ.
Correct.

High nuclear grade and frequent mitoses occur in high-grade ductal carcinoma in situ as well as in invasive tumors. Grade describes how abnormal the cells look and does not show whether they have crossed the basement membrane.

topics: Ductal carcinoma in situ versus invasive ductal carcinoma

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains the strong HER2 staining in this patient's tumor?
options: Point mutation in a nuclear receptor gene
Amplification of a receptor tyrosine kinase gene
Loss of both alleles of a DNA repair gene
Translocation of a kinase gene to a strong promoter
approach: Strong (3+) HER2 staining means the cells make far more receptor than normal.
HER2 is a receptor tyrosine kinase encoded by ERBB2.
In breast cancer, overexpression comes from amplification of ERBB2.
questions.why: HER2 is a transmembrane receptor tyrosine kinase in the EGF receptor family, encoded by ERBB2 on chromosome 17. In about 15 to 20% of breast cancers the gene is amplified into many copies, so the cells overexpress the receptor and receive constant growth signals. Breast cancers are grouped by estrogen receptor, progesterone receptor, and HER2 status: ER-positive tumors form the luminal groups, HER2-amplified tumors form the HER2 group, and tumors negative for all three are triple-negative, a basal-like group linked to BRCA1 mutation. This tumor is ER and PR negative and HER2 positive.
whyNot: Estrogen and progesterone receptors are nuclear receptors, and both are negative in this tumor. HER2 is a cell-surface receptor.
Correct.
Loss of both BRCA1 alleles impairs DNA repair and is linked to triple-negative, basal-like tumors. It does not cause HER2 overexpression.
A translocation that activates a kinase, such as BCR-ABL in chronic myeloid leukemia, is a different mechanism. HER2 is activated by gene amplification.

questions.stem: Lymph from the region of this patient's mass drains mainly to the axillary nodes. Which other lymph node group most directly receives lymph from this region?
options: Parasternal nodes
Deep cervical nodes
Superficial inguinal nodes
Posterior mediastinal nodes
approach: The mass is in the lower inner quadrant, a medial quadrant.
Most breast lymph goes to the axilla, but the medial quadrants also drain medially.
Medial drainage goes to parasternal nodes along the internal thoracic vessels.
questions.why: About 75% of breast lymph, especially from the lateral quadrants, drains to the axillary nodes. Lymph from the medial quadrants, like this lower inner quadrant tumor, also drains to parasternal nodes along the internal thoracic vessels. The blood supply follows a similar pattern: the internal thoracic artery sends perforating branches to the medial breast, and the lateral thoracic and thoracoacromial arteries supply the lateral and upper parts.
whyNot: Correct.
Deep cervical nodes drain the head and neck. Breast lymph reaches the neck only indirectly, through the apical axillary and supraclavicular nodes.
Superficial inguinal nodes drain the lower limb, the perineum, and the skin of the abdominal wall below the umbilicus.
Posterior mediastinal nodes drain the esophagus and posterior mediastinum. They do not receive breast lymph directly.

dx: Invasive lobular carcinoma of the breast in a BRCA2 carrier
case: A 56-year-old woman comes to the physician because of a vague thickening in her right breast that she first noticed 3 months ago. She carries a pathogenic BRCA2 variant, identified after her mother developed ovarian cancer at age 52. Menarche occurred at age 10 and menopause at age 55. She has never been pregnant. Her body mass index is 33 kg/m2. Examination shows an ill-defined area of firmness without a discrete mass in the upper outer quadrant of the right breast. Mammography shows subtle architectural distortion. MRI shows several separate areas of enhancement in the right breast and an 8-mm focus in the left breast. Biopsy of the right breast shows small, uniform cells infiltrating the stroma in single-file strands. The tumor cells do not stain for E-cadherin, are positive for estrogen and progesterone receptors, and are negative for HER2. The diagnosis is invasive lobular carcinoma.

questions.stem: Loss of which of the following functions of the protein absent on immunostaining best explains the growth pattern of this patient's tumor?
options: Calcium-dependent adhesion at adherens junctions
Attachment of cells to laminin in basement membrane
Sealing of the paracellular space at tight junctions
Linkage of keratin filaments at desmosomes
approach: Single-file strands of discohesive cells that lack E-cadherin define invasive lobular carcinoma.
E-cadherin is the calcium-dependent adhesion protein of adherens junctions.
Without it, tumor cells separate and invade the stroma one by one.
questions.why: E-cadherin, encoded by CDH1, is a calcium-dependent transmembrane protein that binds E-cadherin on neighboring cells at adherens junctions and links to the actin cytoskeleton through catenins. Lobular carcinoma loses E-cadherin, so its cells do not stick together. They infiltrate the stroma one by one in single-file lines, form little mass, and are hard to feel or see on mammography. Lobular carcinoma is more often multifocal and bilateral than ductal carcinoma, as in this patient.
whyNot: Correct.
Attachment to laminin in the basement membrane is done by integrins. Integrins are not the protein lost in lobular carcinoma.
Claudins and occludin seal the paracellular space at tight junctions. Their loss makes an epithelium leaky without causing single-file invasion.
Desmogleins and desmocollins link keratin filaments at desmosomes. Antibodies against desmogleins cause pemphigus.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains how this patient's body mass index contributed to her breast cancer risk after menopause?
options: Higher hepatic SHBG production binding more estradiol
Leptin-driven suppression of hypothalamic GnRH release
Insulin-driven increase in ovarian progesterone secretion
Conversion of androgens to estrogen by adipose aromatase
approach: After menopause, the main estrogen source is peripheral aromatization.
Adipose tissue contains aromatase, so more fat means more estrogen.
Longer and higher estrogen exposure of breast epithelium raises cancer risk.
questions.why: After menopause the ovaries make little estradiol, and most estrogen comes from aromatase in adipose tissue, which converts androstenedione to estrone and testosterone to estradiol. More fat therefore means more estrogen, and obesity also lowers SHBG, which raises free estrogen. Prolonged estrogen stimulation of breast epithelium raises cancer risk, which is why early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity, and late first pregnancy are also risk factors. This patient has several of these as well as a BRCA2 variant. Most breast cancers arise in the upper outer quadrant, where most breast tissue lies.
whyNot: Obesity lowers SHBG production by the liver. Higher SHBG would bind more estradiol and reduce its effect.
Leptin signals adequate energy stores and permits GnRH release. After menopause, GnRH cannot raise ovarian estrogen much because few follicles remain.
Ovarian progesterone comes from the corpus luteum after ovulation. After menopause there is no ovulation, so obesity cannot raise it.
Correct.

topics: Estrogen exposure and breast cancer risk

questions.stem: Two years later, this patient's left breast becomes diffusely red, warm, and swollen over several weeks, and its skin develops a pitted, orange-peel texture. She is afebrile, and her leukocyte count is within the reference range. Which of the following best explains these skin changes?
options: Staphylococcal infection of the breast lobules
Tumor emboli in dermal lymphatic vessels
Tumor traction on the suspensory ligaments
Necrosis of breast fat with foamy macrophages
approach: A diffusely red, warm, swollen breast with peau d'orange, no fever, and a normal leukocyte count points to inflammatory carcinoma over mastitis.
Peau d'orange means dermal edema from blocked lymph drainage.
Tumor emboli in dermal lymphatics block that drainage.
questions.why: Inflammatory carcinoma is defined by its clinical picture: a red, warm, swollen breast with peau d'orange. The cause is tumor cells blocking lymphatic vessels in the dermis. Lymph cannot drain, so the skin becomes edematous while staying tethered at the hair follicles, which gives the pitted orange-peel look. There is no infection, abscess, or fever, and the prognosis is poor. Acute mastitis also causes a red, warm breast, but it usually occurs in breastfeeding women with fever, pain, and leukocytosis.
whyNot: S. aureus mastitis usually occurs during breastfeeding and causes fever, pain, and leukocytosis. This patient has none of these.
Correct.
Traction on the suspensory ligaments causes focal skin dimpling over a mass. It does not cause diffuse redness and edema.
Fat necrosis forms a firm mass after trauma, sometimes with dimpling or bruising. It does not cause weeks of spreading redness with peau d'orange.

questions.stem: This patient's 30-year-old son asks about his own risk. Which of the following best describes his chance of having inherited her BRCA2 variant and the cancers for which a male carrier has increased risk?
options: 25%; breast and prostate cancer
25%; testicular cancer and lymphoma
50%; breast and prostate cancer
50%; testicular cancer and lymphoma
approach: BRCA2 cancer predisposition is autosomal dominant, so each child has a 50% chance of inheriting the variant.
BRCA2 is a homologous recombination repair gene, and a tumor forms when the second allele is lost.
In men, BRCA2 raises the risk of breast and prostate cancer.
questions.why: BRCA2 cancer predisposition is inherited as an autosomal dominant trait, so each child of a carrier has a 50% chance of inheriting the variant, whatever the child's sex. BRCA2 helps repair double-strand DNA breaks by homologous recombination, loading RAD51 onto damaged DNA, and a tumor forms when the remaining normal allele is lost in a cell. BRCA1 and BRCA2 carriers have high risks of breast and ovarian cancer. BRCA2 carriers, including men, also have increased risks of male breast cancer, prostate cancer, and pancreatic cancer.
whyNot: A 25% chance fits a child of two carriers of an autosomal recessive trait. BRCA2 cancer predisposition is autosomal dominant.
Both parts are wrong. BRCA2 predisposition is autosomal dominant, and testicular cancer and lymphoma are not BRCA2-related cancers.
Correct.
The 50% chance is right, but testicular cancer and lymphoma are not BRCA2-related cancers.

dx: Benign prostatic hyperplasia with urinary retention
case: A 71-year-old man is brought to the emergency department because he has been unable to urinate for 14 hours and has lower abdominal pain. For 3 years he has had a hesitant, weak urinary stream, a feeling of incomplete emptying, and nocturia three times nightly. Temperature is 36.8 °C (98.2 °F), pulse is 96/min, respirations are 18/min, and blood pressure is 152/88 mmHg. A tender, distended bladder is palpable above the pubic symphysis. Digital rectal examination shows a smooth, firm, rubbery, symmetrically enlarged prostate without nodules. Catheterization drains 1,100 mL of urine. Serum urea nitrogen is 34 mg/dL (7 to 20), and creatinine is 1.9 mg/dL (0.7 to 1.3). Serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is 5.1 ng/mL (less than 4.0). Ultrasonography shows bilateral mild hydronephrosis and a thick-walled bladder. The diagnosis is benign prostatic hyperplasia with acute urinary retention.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the process that enlarged this patient's prostate?
options: Clonal growth of malignant acini in the peripheral zone
Scarring of the gland after chronic bacterial infection
DHT-driven nodules of periurethral glands and stroma
Enlargement of existing cells without new cell division
approach: An older man with obstructive voiding symptoms and a smooth, rubbery, enlarged prostate has benign prostatic hyperplasia.
It is hyperplasia of both glands and stroma, beginning in the periurethral transition zone.
Its growth is driven by DHT made locally from testosterone.
questions.why: Benign prostatic hyperplasia is an increase in the number of both glandular and stromal cells, which form nodules. It begins in the transition zone and periurethral glands around the prostatic urethra, so even modest growth narrows the urethra and causes obstructive symptoms. Growth depends on DHT, made from testosterone by 5-alpha-reductase in prostatic stromal cells, which stimulates growth factors and reduces cell death. It is very common with age and is not a precursor of prostate carcinoma. PSA can be mildly raised because there is more prostatic tissue.
whyNot: Prostate carcinoma usually arises in the peripheral zone and feels hard and nodular on rectal examination. This prostate is smooth and rubbery.
Chronic prostatitis can cause scarring, but it does not produce a diffusely enlarged, rubbery gland made of hyperplastic nodules.
Correct.
Enlargement of existing cells without division is hypertrophy, as in this patient's thickened bladder wall. The prostate in this condition grows by adding new cells.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains this patient's elevated serum creatinine concentration?
options: Raised hydrostatic pressure in Bowman space
Reduced renal blood flow from volume depletion
Immune complex deposits in the glomeruli
Ascending infection destroying renal tubules
approach: Bilateral hydronephrosis with a large retained bladder volume points to obstruction below the bladder.
Backed-up urine raises pressure in the tubules and Bowman space.
That pressure opposes filtration, lowering GFR and raising creatinine (postrenal injury).
questions.why: Prostatic obstruction keeps the bladder from emptying. Pressure builds back through the ureters and renal pelvis (hydronephrosis) into the tubules and Bowman space. Higher pressure in Bowman space opposes filtration, so GFR falls and creatinine and urea rise. This is postrenal kidney injury, and it improves once the obstruction is relieved. Chronic obstruction also thickens the bladder wall through smooth muscle hypertrophy and raises the risk of infection and stones from urinary stasis.
whyNot: Correct.
Volume depletion lowers glomerular capillary pressure and causes prerenal injury. Nothing suggests volume loss here, and he has hydronephrosis from obstruction.
Immune complex glomerulonephritis causes hematuria, proteinuria, and kidney injury without hydronephrosis.
Pyelonephritis can complicate urinary stasis, but he has no fever, and infection would not explain bilateral hydronephrosis.

questions.stem: During this patient's digital rectal examination, the examiner's finger palpates the prostate through which of the following?
options: Posterior wall of the rectum
Peritoneum of the rectovesical pouch
Perineal membrane in the urogenital triangle
Anterior wall of the rectum
approach: Picture a sagittal section: bladder on top, prostate below it, rectum behind both.
The finger enters through the anus and presses forward.
It meets the prostate through the anterior rectal wall.
questions.why: The prostate lies below the bladder, above the perineal membrane, and directly in front of the rectum, separated from it only by the rectoprostatic (Denonvilliers) fascia. A finger in the rectum presses forward through the anterior rectal wall onto the posterior surface of the prostate. The finger enters through the anus in the anal triangle, the posterior part of the diamond-shaped perineum bounded by the pubic symphysis, ischiopubic rami, ischial tuberosities, sacrotuberous ligaments, and coccyx.
whyNot: The posterior rectal wall faces the sacrum and coccyx. The prostate lies in front of the rectum.
The rectovesical pouch is the lowest part of the peritoneal cavity in men and lies above the prostate, between the bladder and rectum. The prostate is below the peritoneum.
The perineal membrane lies below the prostate in the urogenital triangle. A rectal examination enters through the anal triangle.
Correct.

questions.stem: Growth of this patient's prostate depends on an androgen formed from testosterone within the gland. A 46,XY individual with congenital deficiency of the enzyme that forms this androgen would most likely have which of the following?
options: Female external genitalia, no uterus, and sparse hair
Ambiguous genitalia at birth, virilizing at puberty
Normal male genitalia and absent vasa deferentia
Male genitalia with a uterus and uterine tubes
approach: The androgen made in the prostate from testosterone is DHT, formed by 5-alpha-reductase.
In the fetus, DHT masculinizes the external genitalia and prostate, while testosterone drives the Wolffian ducts.
Without the enzyme, the genitalia are ambiguous at birth, and the large rise in testosterone at puberty causes virilization.
questions.why: 5-alpha-reductase type 2 converts testosterone to dihydrotestosterone (DHT) in the prostate and genital skin. In the fetus, DHT forms the penis, scrotum, and prostate, while testosterone itself drives the Wolffian ducts, so the epididymis, vas deferens, and seminal vesicles form normally. A 46,XY infant with 5-alpha-reductase deficiency has ambiguous or female-appearing external genitalia at birth. At puberty, the large rise in testosterone causes virilization with muscle growth and phallic enlargement. The prostate stays small, showing that prostate growth depends on DHT.
whyNot: Female external genitalia, no uterus, and sparse pubic and axillary hair describe complete androgen insensitivity from a defective androgen receptor. Anti-Mullerian hormone still causes Mullerian regression.
Correct.
Absent vasa deferentia with otherwise normal male genitalia occur with CFTR mutations in cystic fibrosis.
A uterus and uterine tubes in a 46,XY male with normal external genitalia result from a lack of anti-Mullerian hormone or its receptor (persistent Mullerian duct syndrome).

case: A 64-year-old man comes to the emergency department because of a 2-day history of fever, shaking chills, painful urination, urinary frequency, and aching pain in the perineum and lower back. Temperature is 39.4 °C (102.9 °F), pulse is 112/min, respirations are 20/min, and blood pressure is 126/76 mmHg. Gentle digital rectal examination shows a warm, swollen, exquisitely tender, boggy prostate. Leukocyte count is 17,600/mm3 (4,500 to 11,000) with increased neutrophils. Urinalysis shows positive leukocyte esterase, positive nitrite, and more than 50 leukocytes per high-power field. Serum prostate-specific antigen (PSA) is 18 ng/mL (less than 4.0). Urine and blood cultures are pending. The diagnosis is acute bacterial prostatitis.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the organism most likely to grow from this patient's urine culture?
options: Gram-negative intracellular diplococcus
Lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod
Obligate intracellular gram-negative bacterium
Coagulase-negative gram-positive coccus
approach: An older man with fever, dysuria, and a tender, boggy prostate has acute bacterial prostatitis.
In older men the cause is the usual urinary pathogens, and a positive nitrite test points to Enterobacterales.
The most likely isolate is E. coli, a lactose-fermenting gram-negative rod.
questions.why: In older men, acute bacterial prostatitis is usually caused by the same organisms that cause urinary tract infections, most often E. coli and other gram-negative rods. They reach the prostate by reflux of infected urine into the prostatic ducts. A positive nitrite test fits, because Enterobacterales such as E. coli reduce urinary nitrate to nitrite. In younger, sexually active men, N. gonorrhoeae and C. trachomatis are more likely causes.
whyNot: N. gonorrhoeae, a gram-negative intracellular diplococcus, causes prostatitis mainly in younger sexually active men. A 64-year-old man with a positive nitrite test most likely has a gut-derived gram-negative rod.
Correct.
C. trachomatis is an obligate intracellular bacterium that causes urethritis and prostatitis mainly in younger sexually active men. It does not grow on routine urine culture.
Coagulase-negative staphylococci such as S. epidermidis infect catheters and prosthetic devices. They are uncommon causes of acute prostatitis.

questions.stem: Over the next 2 years, this patient has three episodes of cystitis caused by the same strain of E. coli, with sterile urine between episodes. He has no pelvic pain between episodes. Which of the following best explains this pattern?
options: Reinfection with new strains from a sexual partner
Autoimmune inflammation of the prostate without bacteria
Bacteria persisting in prostatic ducts that reseed urine
Hematogenous seeding of the bladder from a distant focus
approach: The same organism in repeated episodes, with sterile urine in between, means a hidden reservoir is reseeding the urine.
In men the classic reservoir is the prostate.
This pattern defines chronic bacterial prostatitis, which differs from acute prostatitis and from nonbacterial pelvic pain.
questions.why: Chronic bacterial prostatitis develops when bacteria survive in the prostate, often in ducts or small prostatic stones where they are hard to clear. They periodically reseed the bladder, so the man has recurrent urinary tract infections with the same organism and sterile urine in between. Acute bacterial prostatitis is a sudden febrile illness with a tender, boggy gland. Chronic nonbacterial prostatitis (chronic pelvic pain syndrome) causes pelvic or perineal pain for months with no bacteria found.
whyNot: Reinfection would bring different strains over time. Repeated infection with the identical strain points to a persistent source.
Chronic pelvic pain with no bacteria found fits chronic nonbacterial prostatitis. This patient has proven bacterial infections and no pain between episodes.
Correct.
The bladder is rarely seeded through the blood. Urinary infections in men usually ascend from the urethra or come from a prostatic source.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes the normal function of the protein measured in this patient's serum and the reason its level is high?
options: Liquefies semen; leaks from inflamed glands
Liquefies semen; made only by carcinoma cells
Supplies fructose to sperm; leaks from inflamed glands
Coagulates semen; made by the seminal vesicles
approach: PSA is a serine protease from prostatic epithelium that liquefies the semen coagulum.
It normally stays in the ducts, and little reaches the blood.
Inflammation breaks the epithelial barrier, so PSA leaks into serum.
questions.why: PSA is a serine protease made by prostatic epithelial cells and secreted into the ducts. It breaks down semenogelin, the clotting protein from the seminal vesicles, and liquefies the semen coagulum after ejaculation. Normally little PSA crosses into the blood. Inflammation disrupts the epithelium and basement membrane, so PSA leaks into the circulation, which is why PSA rises in prostatitis and benign hyperplasia as well as in carcinoma. Prostatic fluid also adds citrate and zinc, and the seminal vesicles supply fructose.
whyNot: Correct.
Benign prostatic epithelium makes PSA too. It is specific to the prostate but not to cancer, so infection and benign hyperplasia also raise it.
Fructose for sperm comes from the seminal vesicles. PSA is a protease.
Semenogelin from the seminal vesicles forms the coagulum. PSA comes from the prostate and dissolves the coagulum.

questions.stem: After the infection resolves, his PSA will be rechecked because prostate carcinoma is a concern at his age. Which of the following describes the prostatic zone where most carcinomas arise?
options: Transition zone, around the urethra
Central zone, around the ejaculatory ducts
Anterior fibromuscular stroma, lacking glands
Peripheral zone, toward the rectum
approach: Recall the three glandular zones: peripheral, transition, and central.
Most carcinomas arise in the peripheral zone, which lies posteriorly and laterally.
That position is why carcinomas can be felt on rectal examination and cause urinary symptoms late.
questions.why: The prostate has three glandular zones. The peripheral zone is the largest, holding about 70% of the glandular tissue, and lies posteriorly and laterally, next to the rectum. Most carcinomas begin here, so they can be felt as hard nodules on rectal examination and often cause few urinary symptoms early. The transition zone surrounds the proximal prostatic urethra and is where benign prostatic hyperplasia begins. The central zone surrounds the ejaculatory ducts and is rarely the origin of disease.
whyNot: The transition zone surrounds the proximal prostatic urethra and is the site of benign prostatic hyperplasia, which is why hyperplasia causes urinary obstruction early.
The central zone surrounds the ejaculatory ducts and is an uncommon site of both hyperplasia and carcinoma.
The anterior fibromuscular stroma has no glands, so it does not give rise to adenocarcinoma.
Correct.
